articles.title: How We Saw God’s Goodness Through Our Child’s Cancer
articles.summary: It was not in the good moments where God’s care was most evident. It was in the dark moments, often at night, when we were unsure if our son would survive.
articles.summary_zh: 这不是在神的关怀最明显的美好时刻。在黑暗的时刻，通常是在晚上，我们不确定我们的儿子是否能活下来。
articles.title_zh: 我们如何从孩子的癌症中看到神的良善
articles.content: To encounter profound suffering is to wrestle with isolation. From Job’s seat in the ashes to your neighbor’s loss, news of suffering often includes a struggle to connect. Our family’s cancer journey was like that. We felt alone. And we sensed disconnection—even helplessness—from people who heard the news. Childhood cancer is a blessedly uncommon experience, but navigating pain is inherent to life in a fallen world. When we encounter others’ pain, we have a “Good Samaritan choice”—to step forward and show compassion or to walk away. Nightmare Our 3-year-old son, Ben, had an unexplained illness. After a week in the hospital, we were ushered into an ICU conference room full of doctors and nurses. They delivered the news: “Your son has cancer.” One of the nurses was crying before they even said a word. Our family is from Washington, DC, but we were about 10,000 miles from home. We’d been serving as missionaries in Costa Rica, yet we weren’t there either. On that January day, we were in a hospital in Sydney, Australia, on our dream trip—a family Christmas in summertime. It was quickly becoming a nightmare. The days after the diagnosis were filled with rapid changes. We couldn’t go back to Costa Rica. Returning to DC was almost impossible. The Ronald McDonald House was our new home. My daughter started kindergarten at a new school, in a new country. She drew a picture of her family. There was no home, garden, or pets—just a hospital bed. Ben on his last day of chemotherapy / Courtesy of Peter Morris Over the next six months, Ben endured 96 nights in the hospital, 25 general anesthetics, and chemotherapy so strong it could blind or even kill an adult. He was traveling through the metaphorical valley of the shadow of death, and it was decorated with bright colors and superhero stickers. May 22 is a day we still celebrate in our family as “no more chemo day.” Ben took his final dose of chemotherapy, and we rejoiced with a trip to McDonald’s and a chocolate cake. Despite the celebration, the years ahead held mortal peril. His doctor told us relapse was a risk without a treatment plan. All we could do was watch and wait. Ben was immunocompromised for the years that followed, extending into the 2020s when the disruption of a health crisis—previously rare—became globally mundane. Today, Ben’s body still carries the scars of his cancer and the side effects of the lifesaving treatment he received. But he’s a survivor. To any passerby, he looks like an ordinary 12-year-old boy. My wife and I have scars too. But we also carry the lessons the Lord taught us along the way. Those lessons are available to all believers as we encounter the pain of others. Here are three that stand out. 1. You can’t depend on people. Suffering has an odd way of resetting relationships. We saw it repeatedly, in our experience and with other cancer families we met. The apparent uniqueness of the suffering—and the emotional reactions it stirred—drove some people away. They wouldn’t, or couldn’t, step close and walk with us. However, those people stepping away opened the door to gospel opportunities for us. Australian hospitals rarely have private rooms, so we spent most of our 96 nights sharing rooms with people from diverse cultures and faiths. As other people pulled back from them, we were able to step forward and hold out the hope of the gospel in a dark and hopeless place. 2. You can depend on people. While some in our life pulled away, others chose to pull close. We were thousands of miles from our church family, but people still found ways to care for us. When we shared the news about Ben’s illness, our Facebook post reached more than 15,000 people around the world. It wasn’t the eyeballs that made a difference but the thoughtful actions. Local believers jumped into action with a meal roster. Costa Rican friends translated our English updates to equip our Spanish-speaking friends to pray. American friends prepared care packages, sent encouraging texts, and came

面对深刻的痛苦就是与孤立相搏。 从乔布在灰烬中的座位到邻居的损失, 我们家族的癌症旅程就是这样。 我们感到孤独。 我们感到与那些听到消息的人断绝关系,甚至是无助的。

童年时期的癌症是一种吉祥的罕见经历,但航海痛苦是堕落世界中生命所固有的. 当我们遇到其他人的痛苦时,我们有一个“好撒玛利亚人的选择”——站出来表示同情或离开。 噩梦我们3岁的儿子,本,有一个无法解释的疾病。 在医院里呆了一个星期后,我们被带入了一个由医生和护士组成的ICU会议室.

他们播下了一个消息:“你的儿子得了癌症。 其中一个护士甚至还没说一句话就哭了. 我们的家庭来自华盛顿特区 但我们离家约一万英里 我们一直担任哥斯达黎加的传教士, 1月当天,我们在澳大利亚悉尼的一家医院进行梦想之旅——夏天是家庭圣诞节。

它很快变成了一场噩梦。 诊断后的几天充满了快速的变化. 我们无法回到哥斯达黎加。 返回华盛顿几乎是不可能的。 罗纳德麦当劳之家是我们的新家 我女儿在新学校开始上幼儿园, 在新国家。 她画了一张她家人的照片。 没有家,没有花园,也没有宠物,只有一张医院床。

本最后一天的化疗 / 彼得・莫里斯的礼仪 在接下来的六个月里,本在医院忍受了96个晚上,25个一般麻醉药,化疗如此强大,可以盲目甚至杀死成人. 他穿梭在死亡阴影的隐喻山谷中,装饰着明亮的颜色和超级英雄贴纸.

5月22日仍是我们家庭庆祝的一天, Ben接受了最后的化疗, 尽管有庆典, 未来的岁月仍然有致命的危险。 他的医生告诉我们 复发是一种风险 没有治疗计划。 我们能做的就是观察和等待。

其后的几年里,本被免疫妥协,一直延续到2020年代,以前罕见的一次健康危机的破坏成为全球风云。 今天,Ben的身体仍带有癌症的伤疤和他接受救生治疗的副作用。 但他是个幸存者。 对于任何路人来说,他看起来像一个普通的12岁男孩. 我妻子和我也有伤疤

但我们也带着上帝教给我们的教训 当我们遇到其他人的痛苦时,所有信徒都可以接受这些教训。 这是三个突出的。 1. 你不能依赖人。 受苦有怪异的重构关系方式. 我们从我们的经验和我们遇到的其他癌症家庭中反复看到。

痛苦的明显独特性——以及它激起的情绪反应——驱赶一些人。 他们不会或无法靠近我们, 然而,那些走开的人为我们带来了机会。 澳大利亚的医院很少有私人房间,因此我们在96个晚上的大部分时间都与来自不同文化和信仰的人共用房间.

当其他人从他们那里撤退时,我们得以挺身而出,在一个黑暗和无望的地方抓住福音的希望。 2. 你可以依赖人。 在我们生命中有些人被拉走时,另一些人选择拉近。 我们离教会家数千英里 但人们仍然想方设法照顾我们

articles.source: Wycliffe Bible Translators · 译经故事
articles.summary: Ken and Sally discovered a way to give God’s Word — a gift they’d had access to their whole lives — to others.    The post  Living Out a Legacy of Stewardship and Faith  appeared first on  Wycliffe .
articles.summary_zh: Ken和Sally发现了一种方法，可以将上帝的话语--这是他们一生都能接触到的礼物--传递给他人。“活出管理和信仰的遗产”一文首次出现在威克里夫。
articles.title_zh: 活出管理和信仰的遗产
articles.content: What did your journey to faith look like? Perhaps it was a story of how God showed up in the midst of uncertainty, doubt or fears. Maybe it involved Him seeking you out and rescuing you. Or maybe you grew up in a Christian household and your story is a bit different — perhaps your family regularly read the Bible together and have always known about Jesus’ love. Ken Trager was raised that way. He reflected, “I think when you’re raised in a Christian home … and you have the routines of a life that is built around church and prayer, you just take it for granted.” He added, “It was just the air I breathed.” For Ken and his wife, Sally, faith was always part of their stories. They were each raised in Christian homes, followed Christ, got baptized and had parents who faithfully modeled church attendance, prayer and generosity.  Ken and Sally’s paths eventually crossed at Greenville University in southern Illinois, where they met and fell in love. They went on to build a life centered around family, faith and service. Ken spent his career as a teacher and coach while Sally worked as an accountant, and together they raised two children. Now retired, they’ve moved to be closer to their children and grandchildren, giving them a new opportunity to pour into the next generation. Through all those years and seasons, the faith Ken and Sally had seen modeled by their families continued to shape their home. Early in their marriage, Ken and Sally met a mentor who encouraged the couple to go deeper with their faith — to study Scripture, ask questions and wrestle honestly with what they believed. It was an important season of discovering that the faith that had been passed down from their families could also become something they personally owned and lived out together. What Do You Take for Granted? Years later, the couple experienced an aha moment when they were introduced to Wycliffe at an event. There, Ken and Sally heard story after story from people who had received Scripture in their own languages. Something clicked for Sally: “We’ve never known a day where we couldn’t access the Bible. And these people have just longed for it, and they’re finally getting it.” For the first time, something that had always surrounded the couple became visible — and it was a gift they could no longer take for granted . Ken and Sally had spent years thinking about the importance of God’s Word. Seeing people receive Scripture in their own languages helped them understand just how extraordinary that access is. “The power of salvation comes through that,” Ken said. “I can’t think of … [a more] important work than providing God’s Word to everybody in the world.” Sally agreed. “To have His Word is as if we’re hearing the voice of God,” she said. “God works through His Word.” This conviction — for people around the world to be able to access Scripture for themselves — became one of the reasons Ken and Sally prioritized a place in their giving for Wycliffe. But it also became part of a larger question about generosity they had been asking themselves for years: “If everything we have is a gift from God, what does it look like to live generously with it?” A Generous Heart Generosity, like faith, was something Ken and Sally had grown up around. Ken remembers his dad giving him money to put in the offering plate, and Sally remembers watching her parents give not just to their church but to people and organizations in need. Sally’s father especially enjoyed giving anonymously. As Ken and Sally have grown older, they’ve learned that generosity isn’t simply about giving a certain percentage or checking a box; it’s about continually asking what it means to have a generous heart . 你的信仰之旅是什么样子的? 也许这是上帝如何在不确定、怀疑或恐惧中出现的故事。 也许这涉及到他寻找你 并救你。 或者你在一个基督教家庭长大,你的故事有点不同——也许你的家人经常一起阅读圣经,并且一直知道耶稣的爱。 肯崔格是那样长大的

他回想道 , “ 我想当你在基督教家庭长大... 你有一个在教堂和祷告周围建造的日常生活, 你只是把它视为理所当然。 ” 他又说:“只是我呼吸的空气。” 对于肯和他的妻子莎莉来说,信仰总是他们的故事的一部分.

他们各自在基督教家中长大,跟随基督,接受洗礼,并有忠实的模范教会出席,祈祷和慷慨的父母. 肯和莎莉的道路最终在伊利诺伊州南部的格林维尔大学交叉,在那里他们相遇并坠入爱河. 他们继续建立一个以家庭、信仰和服务为中心的生活。

肯在萨利担任会计期间度过了教师和教练的生涯,两人一起抚养两个孩子. 他们已经退休了, 他们已经搬到更亲近他们的儿孙, 给他们一个新的机会, 注入下一代。 在那些年和季节中,肯和莎莉所见到的由家人塑造的信仰继续塑造自己的家园.

早年的婚姻中,肯和莎莉结识了一位导师,他鼓励这对夫妇更深入地信仰——学习圣经,提出问题,并诚实地与所相信的东西搏斗. 这是一个重要的季节,发现从家人传下来的信仰也可能成为他们个人拥有和共同生活的东西. 你拿什么给格兰特?

多年后,夫妇俩在一次活动上被介绍到怀克利夫(Wycliffe)时,经历了一段愉快的时刻. 在那里,肯和莎莉从以自己语言接受圣经的人那里听到一个接一个的故事. “我们从未知道有一天我们无法阅读圣经。

而这些人也只是渴望, 第一次,一直包围着这对夫妇的东西变得明显——这是他们不能再视为理所当然的礼物了. 肯和莎莉花了多年时间思考上帝之言的重要性.

看到人们用自己的语言接受圣经 有助于他们理解这种访问是多么非凡 肯说,“救赎的力量来自此”。 " 我无法想象......比向全世界每个人提供上帝的话更重要的工作。 " 萨莉同意了 ”她说,

“真主通过他的话而工作。” 这种信念——让世界各地的人们能够为自己获得圣经——成为肯和莎莉在为威克利夫奉献一个位置时优先考虑的原因之一.

但是,它也成为了一个更大的问题的一部分,即他们多年来一直问自己:“如果我们所拥有的一切是上帝的礼物,那么与它慷慨相处是什么样子?” 和信仰一样 善良的心是肯和莎莉成长的

肯记得父亲给了他钱放进祭品盘中,莎莉记得看着她的父母不仅把钱送给他们的教堂,还送给需要帮助的人和组织. Sally的父亲特别喜欢匿名赠送。 肯和莎莉已经长大了, 他们已经了解到慷慨不只是给予一定的百分比或检查一个盒子。

需要不断问, 对肯来说,慷慨意味着什么的问题已经变成了他所谓的“提高国王地位”的问题。 当他考虑施舍的时候,他问道:"这难道是为了真主的荣耀而推动王国吗? 这个问题决定了夫妻双方对哪些个人和组织的看法

articles.title: Finding Wonder in the Midst of Christmas Weariness
articles.source: Wycliffe Bible Translators · 译经故事
articles.summary: Rediscover the wonder of Christmas by focusing on God’s faithfulness and the hope found in Jesus.   The post  Finding Wonder in the Midst of Christmas Weariness  appeared first on  Wycliffe .
articles.summary_zh: 通过关注神的信实和耶稣的盼望，重新发现圣诞节的奇迹。“在圣诞节疲惫中寻找奇迹”一文首次出现在威克里夫。
articles.title_zh: 在圣诞节疲惫中寻找奇迹
articles.content: Christmas is supposed to be a season of wonder. Twinkling lights, familiar songs, meaningful traditions and time with people you love can all point toward the joy of celebrating Jesus’ birth. But when your December calendar fills with responsibilities and expectations, weariness can settle in before you realize it. Maybe you remember a time when Christmas felt different. As a child, you may have counted down the days and experienced joy in even the smallest traditions. As an adult, you might find yourself simply trying to catch your breath as you move from one responsibility to the next. In the middle of trying to make Christmas special for everyone else, it can be easy to miss the wonder yourself. But the Christmas story gives you an opportunity to slow down and remember what this season is really about. In Luke 1, before the story of Jesus’ birth begins, you meet people who knew what it meant to wait, wonder and trust that God was at work even when they couldn’t yet see what He was doing. Weary of Waiting Luke’s account of the life of Jesus doesn’t begin with Jesus’ birth; it begins instead with the story of Zechariah, an elderly priest who was tired of waiting. Zechariah had heard promises of Israel’s rescue from oppression and sin his entire life. That future must have seemed out of reach under Rome’s harsh control. But Zechariah and his wife, Elizabeth, also had an unfulfilled personal longing: “They had no children because Elizabeth was unable to conceive, and they were both very old” ( Luke 1:7, NLT ). One day, as Zechariah performed his duties in the temple, he was chosen to burn incense in the sanctuary — a rare honor with an unexpected result: While Zechariah was in the sanctuary, an angel of the Lord appeared to him, standing to the right of the incense altar. Zechariah was shaken and overwhelmed with fear when he saw him. But the angel said, “Don’t be afraid, Zechariah! God has heard your prayer. Your wife, Elizabeth, will give you a son, and you are to name him John. You will have great joy and gladness, and many will rejoice at his birth, for he will be great in the eyes of the Lord. He must never touch wine or other alcoholic drinks. He will be filled with the Holy Spirit, even before his birth. And he will turn many Israelites to the Lord their God. He will be a man with the spirit and power of Elijah. He will prepare the people for the coming of the Lord. He will turn the hearts of the fathers to their children, and he will cause those who are rebellious to accept the wisdom of the godly” ( Luke 1:11-17, NLT ). Trusting God in the Waiting An angel of the Lord appeared to Zechariah and announced that God had heard his prayer. Elizabeth would have a son named John who would “… prepare the people for the coming of the Lord” ( Luke 1:17b, NLT ). After years of waiting, God answered Zechariah and Elizabeth’s prayer as part of an even bigger story: They would finally have the child they had prayed for, and their son would prepare the way for Jesus. But Zechariah struggled to understand how it could possibly happen: “… ‘How can I be sure this will happen? I’m an old man now, and my wife is also well along in years’” ( Luke 1:18, NLT ). Zechariah could only see what seemed possible based on his circumstances. But God was asking him to trust what He had promised. The angel Gabriel responded by telling Zechariah that he would be unable to speak until the child was born, adding, “For my words will certainly be fulfilled at the proper time” ( Luke 1:20b, NLT ). Maybe you know what it’s like to pray about something for months or even years. It can be hard to keep trusting that God is working when it seems like nothing is changing. Zechariah’s story reminds us that even when we can’t see what God is doing, He is still faithful to His promises. Waiting is woven throughout the Christmas story. Maybe it’s part of your story too. 圣诞节应该是奇迹的季节 闪烁的灯光、熟悉的歌曲、有意义的传统和时间, 但当您12月的日历充满了责任和期望时,疲惫可以在您意识到之前安顿下来. 也许你记得圣诞节感觉不一样的时候

作为一个孩子,你可能已经 计数的日子和体验快乐 即使最小的传统。 作为一个成年人,你可能会发现自己只是 试图呼吸 当你从一个责任转移到下一个责任。 在试图让圣诞节对其他人特别的时候,自己也很容易错过奇迹.

但圣诞故事给了你一个机会,让你慢下来,并记住本季的真正内容. 在卢卡斯一世,耶稣诞生的故事开始前,你遇见了那些知道等待、好奇和相信上帝在工作的意义的人,即使他们还看不到他在做什么。 等待卢克对耶稣生活的描述,

以撒迦利亚的故事开始 撒迦利亚是一位老牧师 他厌倦了等待 撒迦利亚曾听到过以色列从压迫中解救出来的承诺,他一生都有罪。 罗马的严酷控制下,这一未来似乎已遥不可及。

但是,Zachariah和他的妻子Elizabeth也有未实现的个人愿望:“他们没有孩子,因为Elizabeth无法怀孕,而且他们都非常老”(Luke 1:7, NLT)。

一天,当撒迦利亚在圣殿中履行职责时,他被选中在圣殿烧香——这是罕见的荣誉,结果出乎意料:撒迦利亚在圣殿时,上帝的天使出现在他面前,站在香坛的右边. 撒迦利亚见到他时,被震撼和恐惧所压倒. 但天使说:"撒迦利亚,不要害怕!

他将是一个拥有以利亚精神和力量的人。 他会为主的到来为人民做准备. 他将把父亲们的心转向他们的孩子,他将使那些叛逆的人接受神的智慧”(Luke 1:11-17,NLT). 相信上帝在等待上帝的天使出现在撒迦利亚面前,并宣布上帝听到了他的祈祷.

Elizabeth将有一个名叫John的儿子,他将“为主的到来为人民做好准备”(Luke 1:17b, NLT)。 经过多年的等待,上帝回答了撒迦利亚和伊丽莎白的祈祷,作为更大的故事的一部分: 他们最终会有他们祈祷的孩子,他们的儿子会为耶稣准备道路.

但撒迦利亚却挣扎着去理解这怎么可能发生:“......我怎么能肯定这会发生呢? 我已是老人, Zachariah只能从他的情况看出什么是可能的。 但上帝要求他相信他所承诺的

天使Gabriel在回答时告诉Zachariah, 在孩子出生之前, 他无法说话, 并补充说, “我的话一定会在适当的时候实现”(Luke 1:20b, NLT)。 也许你知道祈祷几个月甚至几年是什么感觉。 很难继续相信上帝在工作 似乎没什么变化

撒迦利亚的故事提醒我们,即使我们看不到上帝在做什么,他仍然忠实于他的诺言。 等待被编织 整个圣诞节的故事。 也许这也是你的故事的一部分。 我们的四周免费的礼拜,“期待在等待中”,可以帮助你在《圣经》中度过时间。

articles.title: No Incomplete Stories: God’s Word for All People
articles.source: Wycliffe Bible Translators · 译经故事
articles.summary: See how Bible translation helps communities access more of God’s Word through print, audio and sign language Scripture today.   The post  No Incomplete Stories: God’s Word for All People  appeared first on  Wycliffe .
articles.summary_zh: 了解圣经翻译如何帮助社区通过印刷、音频和手语圣经获得更多上帝的话语。《No Incomplete Stories: God's Word for All People》一文首先出现在《Wycliffe》上。
articles.title_zh: 没有不完整的故事：上帝给所有人的话语
articles.content: Imagine reading a book, watching a show or listening to a podcast when suddenly the story just stops mid-sentence. Maybe the previous reader has ripped out a page, the series was canceled before the showrunners could wrap up the plotline, or the producer distributed the episode before realizing it was incomplete. How incredibly frustrating to not experience the full story from start to finish! It can leave us emotionally unsettled, frustrated or even distraught, because at our core, we desire completion. We want to know how things start and how they end. We don’t just want a taste, because it feels like a tease. We’re left wanting more . And we’re not alone in that desire! articles.content: What circumstances or experiences have shaped your life? For 93-year-old Millie (name changed), her testimony was shaped by the Great Depression and deep loss, but also by an enduring faith and a lifetime of seeing God’s faithfulness unfold. Every chapter of her story points back to the same truth: God’s Word sustained her. Millie was only six weeks old when her father suffered severe burns to his legs from an explosion. Overnight, Millie’s mother found herself caring for a newborn and a toddler while tending to a husband who was facing a long and painful recovery. Life was uncertain, and every dollar mattered. Yet when Millie looks back on those difficult years, she doesn’t first remember hardship. She remembers the faith that was demonstrated. Every Sunday morning, Millie’s mother would reach into a small jar where she saved a few quarters and hand one to Millie and one to her sister before they left for church. The family didn’t have much, but her parents believed that honoring God was never dependent on how much they had. “We were taught to tithe,” Millie recalled. “To give to the Lord because of His goodness to us.” Long before Millie understood phrases like “stewardship” or “planned giving,” she was learning a lesson that would shape the rest of her life: Generosity isn’t born out of abundance; it grows from trusting the one who provides. See how God is using the generosity of one group of friends to impact Bible translation → The Scripture Millie Carried Through the Years As Millie grew older, that foundation of faith continued to guide her. She married a godly man, and they centered their efforts around family, teaching and serving others. Both were educators, and they poured themselves into the lives of children while also remaining deeply involved in their church and community. Together, the couple experienced the joys of raising a family. But they also walked through a devastating loss. While Millie was pregnant with their younger son, the couple’s 7-year-old daughter tragically died. It’s difficult to imagine the depth of grief that Millie endured. Through her pain, she turned to God and His Word for comfort. Even now, decades later, she is still anchored by the promises found in Scripture. One particular passage resonates with Millie deeply: You will keep in perfect peace all who trust in you, all whose thoughts are fixed on you! Trust in the LORD always, for the LORD GOD is the eternal Rock. — Isaiah 26:3-4 (NLT) For Millie, Scripture was what met her in her grief, strengthened her through suffering and continued to anchor and guide her throughout the next chapters of her life. Millie believes the Lord’s presence was unmistakable in the moments that followed this event. articles.summary_zh: 伊恩· H ·穆雷（ Iain H. Murray ）的《艾米·卡迈克尔：灰烬之美》（ Amy Carmichael: Beauty for Ashes ）是对爱尔兰传教士前往印度的非凡生活的简短复述。接下来是该标题的第4章， “艰难的日子和黄金岁月。“如果说艾米·卡迈克尔的生活有任何模式的话，那就是令人耳目一新的时代，然后是考验的时代，令人兴奋的‘攀登’的时代[…]艾米·卡迈克尔的帖子：令人耳目一新的时代和考验的时代首先出现在真理美国的旗帜上。

articles.content: Iain H. Murray’s Amy Carmichael: Beauty for Ashes is a short retelling of the remarkable life of the Irish missionary to India. What follows is Chapter 4 of that title, ‘Hard Days and Golden Years.’ If there was any pattern to Amy Carmichael’s life it was of times of refreshing then of trials, of exhilarating ‘climbing’ then of walking in dark ravines. In part her explanation was that demonic activity follows the work of the Holy Spirit. As she quoted from George Bowen, When Christianity assumes an aggressive attitude the first result is a great exhibition of Satanic power. Satan’s power to be manifested must be assaulted. 1 Such an understanding does not come so readily to us who do not live, as she did, within sight of demon possession, or within hearing of tom-tom drums calling devotees to idols. Shortly before Walker 2 had left on his last mission, he had been sitting with Amy and others in deck chairs under the stars. ‘We had been talking’, she later wrote, of work and workers, and of those (to me) most wonderful women, who seemed perfectly self-reliant, needing no strong arm alongside. I remember how, suddenly startled at the bare thought of working alone, in the sense of all the burden of responsibility, I exclaimed that I never could do it. Mr Walker laughed. ‘Well, you don’t have to’, he said. 3 Amy was the weaker when her ‘strong arm’ died at the age of fifty-four. What she owed to Walker’s ‘courageous championship’ of the children’s work, ‘through its first very difficult years, no words can tell, nor can words tell how he is missed’. 4 At times, as she faced her loss, she would need to say to herself, ‘Don’t give up, don’t be afraid: go on.’ Prayer for ‘fortitude’ entered her life. There were unsympathetic neighbours who observed the work at Dohnavur who supposed that Amy would now be more vulnerable. One of these was a lawyer who, soon after Walker’s death, wrote with the demand that current work on the building of a wall around the compoundbe stopped, and that a half-built nursery should be pulled down. They were using ground, he claimed, to which they did not have legal title. ‘He had waited till Mr Walker’s death had left us, as he thought, defenceless, almost desolate, and sure to be easily cowed by threats of court trouble.’ The wall building had been prompted by the passage of a tiger through the compound at night; and the new nursery was necessitated by the growing numbers of children for whom Dohnavur had become home. Amy ignored the letter and heard nothing more of the threat. The Dohnavur family of seventy children and grown-ups in 1906, had doubled itself by this date, and the need of more helpers was pressing. Mrs Catherine Carmichael was never able to return. She died on July 14, 1913. A few weeks earlier a letter from her to Amy began with the words, ‘My own most precious earthly possession’. While Amy did not lament her mother’s death—for no Christian death was to be ‘lamented’—in the days ahead she needed to preach to herself, ‘I must remind myself to live in the joy of those gone, not grovel in the sense of my loss.’ Mrs Carmichael had been a constant supporter and representative for Dohnavur in Britain. She acted as the home secretary to whom gifts could be sent, and helped to make her daughter’s books more widely known. In 1912 those books had been noted by Queen Mary, wife of King George V, who expressed her thanks for them. While Amy was busy in 1913 writing Walker of Tinnevelly , there came the possibility of the loss of her closest female friend and helper, Ponnammal, who had been with her ever since, as a young widow, she had come to new life through Walker’s preaching. She now needed surgery for cancer and Amy went with her to a Salvation Army Hospital at Neyyoor for a period. In their absence from Dohnavur (forty-six miles away), and the absence of Mabel Wade who was on furlough, 70 of the children were ill. articles.content_zh: 伊恩·H·默里所著的"艾米·卡迈克尔:爱希斯的美人"(Amy Carmichael: Beautiful for Ashes)是爱尔兰传教士到印度的出众生的短篇回忆. 下面是该标题的第4章: " 艰难的日子和黄金年 " 。 如果Amy Carmichael的生活有任何规律的话, 她的部分解释是,妖魔活动遵循了圣灵的工作. 正如她从乔治·博文所引述的那样,当基督教采取侵略态度时,第一个结果就是撒旦力量的伟大展览. 必须攻击撒旦的力量。 1 对我们来说,这种理解并不像她那样活在恶魔拥有的目光下,或者在听到汤姆·通鼓呼唤献给偶像的人面前。 在行走者2号执行上个任务前不久,他一直和艾米等人坐在星空下的甲板椅上. 她后来写道:‘我们谈过了',内容是工作和工人,以及那些似乎完全自力更生、不需要任何坚强的手臂的妇女。 我记得,我突然对独自工作的赤裸裸的想法感到惊奇,因为我肩负着所有的责任,我感到惊叹,我永远做不到。 华克先生笑了 他说,你不必这么做。 3 Amy在54岁时死亡, 她对沃克的“勇敢的冠军”儿童工作所负的责任是,“在第一个非常困难的岁月里,言语无法分辨,言语也无法分辨他是如何被错过的”。 页:1 有时,当她面临损失时,她需要对自己说: " 不要放弃,不要害怕:继续吧。 " 祈求`宽恕'进入她的生活。 有不同情的邻居在多赫纳武尔观察作品,他们认为艾米现在会更加脆弱. 其中一个是一位律师,他在Walker死后不久写道,他要求停止目前在大院周围建造一堵墙的工作,应当拆除一个半建的托儿所。 他声称,他们使用了他们没有合法所有权的地盘。 他一直等待着沃克先生的死像他所想的那样离开我们,他手无寸铁,几乎是荒凉的,而且肯定很容易被法庭麻烦的威胁吓倒了。 墙上建筑的动因是一只老虎在夜间穿过大院;新的托儿所是因越来越多的儿童成为家而必需的。 艾米无视信件,没有听到更多的威胁. 1906年有70个孩子和成年人的多赫纳武尔家族,到这时已使自己翻了一番,迫切需要更多的帮助. 凯瑟琳·卡迈克尔夫人一直没能回来 她于1913年7月14日去世. 几周前,她给艾米的一封信开头写道,“我拥有自己最珍贵的地产”。 Amy没有为她母亲的死感到悲哀——因为没有一个基督徒的死是`在她需要为自己传道的几天里感到悲伤',`我必须提醒自己生活在那些死去的人的欢快中,而不是在我失去的意义上的忧郁'。 卡迈克尔夫人一直是英国多赫纳武尔的支持者和代表。 她担任家庭秘书,可以向她寄送礼物,并帮助使她女儿的书更广为人知。 1912年,这些书被乔治五世国王的妻子玛丽王后所注意到,玛丽王后对之表示感谢. 在1913年艾米忙于写作"Tinnevelly"的Walker(Walker of Tinnevelly)时,出现了失去她最亲密的女性朋友和助手Ponnammal(Ponnammal)的可能性,她从那时起就一直与她在一起,作为一个年轻的寡妇,她通过Walker的传道而来到了新的生活. 她现在需要手术治疗癌症,艾米和她一起去内约尔的救世军医院住了一段时间. 在他们离开多克纳武尔(相距四十六里外),而当时在放假的马贝尔·韦德(英语:Mabel Wade (film))不在的情况下,70个孩子生病了. There are needed roles for IMB missionaries in healthcare, ministering to the needs of local populations and utilizing this time to minister to spiritual needs. IMB Photo When most Southern Baptists think of missionaries, they often picture church planters and evangelists. But leaders with the International Mission Board say some of the greatest needs today are for professionals whose work happens behind the scenes. IMB leaders report that critical roles such as teachers, healthcare workers, counselors, accountants, logistics specialists and member care personnel are helping advance the Great Commission in ways many churches never see. Doreen Baker, IMB director of TCK (third culture kid or missionary kid) education, sees a constant need for education professionals. Teachers are needed in international schools, which cover a variety of global educational entities, and in other settings to provide for missionary kids and their educational needs. “Teachers are significant in that not only are they providing instruction for students, but they are an integral part of the core missionary task ,” Baker said. “We also have great needs for consultants to support our families on the field with their children’s education in many ways.” Baker previously served 25 years teaching in Asia and experienced how education creates access to missions where traditional pathways may be limited. IMB missionary Ellie Bohrer teaches a 12th grade World Views class at Black Forest Academy in Germany. The IMB is seeking other educators, like Bohrer, who are willing to use their skills on the mission field. IMB Photo Scott Ray, IMB senior director of global deployment, noted that many missionary positions go unfilled simply because they fall outside traditional perceptions of missionary service. He said professional skills can provide both practical ministry support and access to countries where traditional missionary visas are difficult to obtain. Opportunities exist for finance professionals, veterinarians, medical workers, Send Relief personnel and others. Healthcare remains one of the most strategic areas in demand. Tom Hicks, IMB director of global health strategies, said many medical professionals have the wrong perception about mission work. “We do have an issue where people will select out because they don’t think that what they do is useful on the mission field,” he said. In reality, Hicks said many areas across the globe are increasingly seeking family medicine physicians, internists, pediatricians, pediatric nurse practitioners, OB providers, physical therapists, occupational therapists, speech pathologists and lactation consultants. The need is especially significant in sub-Saharan Africa, where young populations create a growing demand for pediatric care. Healthcare professionals also provide a unique advantage in countries that restrict missionary activity. “Missionaries with a vocational value, like healthcare missionaries, have opportunities to go places that others can’t go,” Hicks said. Another often-overlooked ministry is member care, which focuses on the spiritual, emotional, mental and relational health of IMB missionaries. Chris Martin is the IMB director of global member care. “Member care missionaries stand alongside those missionaries that are thought of traditionally as church planters or evangelists and support them,” Martin said. Many who serve in these roles come from counseling backgrounds and help missionaries navigate stress, conflict, grief and other challenges that can affect long-term ministry effectiveness. Martin compares their role to Aaron and Hur in Exodus 19, holding up Moses’ arms during battle, strengthening those serving on the front lines. articles.content: In South Asia, Maryam and a local pastor baptize Tara, a new believer. IMB missionaries work alongside local believers and churches to fulfill the Great Commission. IMB Photo Twenty minutes had passed already. The sun was going down, and they were looking everywhere, but they only saw men in the park. Sophia, an International Mission Board missionary, joined another IMB missionary and Maryam, a South Asian Christian. They went to the park to share the gospel, but approaching a man in their Muslim-majority city was out of the question. They kept walking and watching. Even if they went home without a single conversation, Sophia knew Maryam would want to try again. This woman who had grown up with a distrust of Muslims, now searched a park for a Muslim woman to tell about Jesus. When Sophia first invited her along, Maryam never imagined a Muslim could come to know Jesus. But the more they went out sharing the gospel together, the more God softened her heart. “One day, I found she was sharing in the park by herself, without me,” Sophia said with a laugh. These days, she shares regularly — with classmates, with rickshaw drivers, with women in the park, when she can find them. God transformed Maryam’s heart. He could transform this walk through the park, too. “So we stopped,” Sophia said, “and prayed, ‘God, give us just one woman to talk to.’” Then they spotted her — a girl sitting alone on a bench. Meeting the girl on the bench She looked like other conservative Muslim women in the area, covered in black except for her face. They approached casually, not wanting to frighten her. It was Eid al-Adha – “one of the biggest Muslim holidays here,” Sophia said. They greeted her and asked about her holiday plans. Her name was Tara, and she wasn’t intimidated at all. “You may think I’m a Muslim from the way I dress,” she said, “but actually in my heart, I have left Islam.” “I was a little shocked,” Sophia said, hearing such a bold statement from a stranger. Tara told them she was a university student at a conservative Islamic school, but she had grown disillusioned and discontent with the religion. “ I don’t believe in Islam anymore,” Tara said. Without knowledge of God, she had no one to pray to, and it left her lonely. She’d been searching — Buddhism and Hinduism from friends, even a meeting with atheists, who struck her as unhappy, following only themselves. “Do you know any Christians?” Sophia asked. “Would you like to hear what we believe?” “Sure, please share.” They read about Jesus’ birth, and Tara was hungry for more. When she asked about church, Sophia described their congregation of about 40 believers, many from a Muslim background. Though she wasn’t ready to visit the church, Tara continued her interest in learning. Sophia and Maryam met with her every week in coffee shops, tea shops, Sophia’s home, wherever they could talkthat wasn’t too loud or have “too many ears and eyes” observing them. Finding her closest friend They read through the Gospel of John. One November day in a coffee shop, they reached the passage on the Samaritan woman at the well, and Sophia noticed Tara was crying. “Tara, I see you have tears,” Sophia said. “Let’s stop. Let’s talk about it .” That day, Tara prayed to receive Christ. Soon after, she wanted to visit the church, though nervous how believers would receive her in a hijab. “They will love you,” Sophia told her. “Don’t worry.” Tara went and was welcomed. That Christmas, 80 people packed Sophia’s apartment, singing and dancing in circles. Across the room, Sophia saw Tara, wearing red Christmas garland like a scarf and a smile stretched across her face. “Tara grew up very conservative – music was not even allowed in her home. But now she’s dancing, worshiping the Lord with us with music and songs.” In South Asia, Maryam and a local pastor baptize Tara, a new believer. articles.content: The eastern face of St. Peter's Basilica in the Vatican City in Rome, Italy, is famous for its central balcony from which popes give their papal addresses. Most people in Rome have at least a cultural connection to Roman Catholicism as the city is “the heart of Catholicism.” IMB Photo In the city where Jason and Lizzy Davis serve, some steps have a lot of meaning. And the meaning is different for them than it is for the thousands who travel there to visit that site. “If you come to Rome, you can come to a place called the Holy Steps,” Jason said. “People go there, and they’ll crawl up on their knees and pray the rosary all the way up.” From the top of the steps, a mural depicting Jesus on the Cross looks down on those making the pilgrimage. For Jason and Lizzy, it’s a spiritual experience, a picture of a religion that asks people to earn their way to Jesus. “That’s really the opposite of what the gospel is. The gospel is Jesus saying, ‘No, you can’t do it . . . no matter how good you think you are,’” they said. Most people in Rome have at the very least a cultural connection to Roman Catholicism, as the city is “the heart of Catholicism.” Jason explained, “It’s where the Pope lives in the Vatican. It’s very much part of the religion and culture. It’s all intertwined here.” An ‘unavoidable’ call Jason and Lizzy are investing their lives as International Mission Board missionaries in Rome, Italy, to share the truth of the gospel. The Davises partner with national believers through a new church plant, and they’re seeking to plant more churches within the city. Lizzy said for her, the call to missions was unavoidable. “I grew up as a third culture kid, or a missionary kid. My parents were on the mission field, as were my grandparents, all with the International Mission Board.” Then her family moved to Virginia for her dad to work for IMB’s home office staff. As a middle schooler and high schooler, every time Lizzy heard about the need for the gospel to go forth, she felt a burden, a “burning” in her heart. She didn’t know what God would do with that, but she had a feeling she would see one day. Now, years later, she and Jason spend their time trying to find as many opportunities as they can to invite people into their home so they can share the hope of Jesus with them. That can mean Bible study or simply sharing a meal. ‘Completely lost’ Jason has been surprised by just how often people are willing to talk about faith. “You can get into spiritual conversations very quickly with people, especially if you’re just open and honest with them.” Lizzy shared that one of the easiest ways to do this is to be willing to let your day be interrupted. “That’s something I’ve seen Jason do firsthand in our neighborhood. Couto is a professional violinist who is serving as a global missionary partner with the IMB in Japan. Doors have opened for her to use her skills with evangel ical Japanese musicians who perform. IMB Photo Rebeca Couto moved from one volcanic archipelago to another, leaving Portugal’s Azores islands to anchor her life in Japan. The percentage of evangelical Christians in the Azores and Japan is similar, with both populations under 1%. Couto is a fourth-generation Christian, a rarity on the small islands. She is one of few, if any, believers in the Azores with such a long spiritual lineage. This rich legacy shaped her and prepared her for ministry. “I’ve always understood the Great Commission as a call for all believers and all disciples of Christ to be missionaries, wherever they are, whatever they’re doing, and whatever God has equipped them with,” Couto said. Couto’s great-grandfather became a Christian through the witness of missionaries from the United Kingdom. Later, missionaries from the Foreign Mission Board, now the International Mission Board, started the first Baptist work in the Azores by planting an English-speaking church near an American military base. A Baptist Brazilian couple planted a Portuguese-speaking church, which became the congregation where Couto grew up and was commissioned as a missionary. Ministry has been passed down through the generations of her family. Couto’s father has pastored for 20 years, and both of her parents have been involved in ministry for most of their lives. Couto now serves in Japan as a global missionary partner, a missionary who is financially supported by a sending church or organization in their home country and serves with IMB teams. Close to 400 GMPs currently serve on IMB teams around the world. Language learning Couto is immersed in language study in Yokohama, Japan. She had a head start before she even arrived. After graduating from high school, Couto moved from the Azores to Lisbon to pursue a degree in music. She spent hours on public transportation and wanted a challenge to pass the time. She decided to study Japanese because she thought it sounded beautiful. At the time, she had no intention of becoming a missionary in the traditional sense. However, the more she learned about the language and the culture, her burden for the lost grew. She began researching Christianity in Japan. “I understood how bleak the scenario was, and how much the country needed Jesus. I struggled with that calling because the doors were closed, and it didn’t seem possible to come to Japan for a myriad of reasons,” Couto said. After finishing master’s degrees in music and violin performance, along with a seminary degree, Couto was considering pursuing a Ph.D. or returning to seminary when her seminary professors, IMB missionaries Jonathan and Bethany Sharp, contacted her about serving as a missionary in Japan. They introduced her to the GMP program and invited her to attend a missions immersion school they piloted . Music to their ears As a professional violinist, Couto brought her violin to Japan, unsure of what opportunities existed, but she knew her call to the mission field somehow involved her gifting. “I see myself as having been called to serve through music. I never even conceived doing missions while excluding the violin entirely,” Couto said. She continued, “Music is such a universal way to connect with people, and it’s so intuitive to pair that with the gospel and with God’s message to people’s hearts.” While she knew the Lord would somehow open a door for her to use the violin for kingdom work, she was at peace with the possibility that, for a season, she may not be as active in music. articles.content: Men and women gather to discuss spiritual topics with Caleb and Carina Beaty, International Mission Board missionaries who serve in Madrid. IMB Photo Across Spain, people looking for connection and meaningful conversation turn to the internet to find groups where they can meet others. At a café by the river, Caleb and Carina Beaty engage in conversations about finding purpose, beauty and “what’s wrong with the world.” A website called Meetup allows people to search for groups to meet in person. The description of the Beatys’ group indicates that it discusses spiritual topics. People come expecting to talk about faith, so it’s not a surprise when they arrive. Caleb said he always has a list of questions that begin broadly and funnel into questions such as, “If there were a God …” or “What do you think Christians believe about that?” or “Why do you think religions have such different perspectives?” The Beatys’ goal in these conversations is to work toward deeper worldview questions within 45 minutes to an hour. Most of the people who attend their Meetup group are from Madrid, but they also have conversations with people from other countries. During one Meetup, Caleb and Carina shared how creation was perfect, but sin led to a world separated from the Father. God offers salvation through the death and resurrection of Jesus, they explained. “There are times we’re able to get to a clear gospel presentation with a group of people, and sometimes we’re doing pre-evangelism.” Caleb said. Some repeat attendees who have been attending for more than a year quickly jump to the heart of the discussion. “All right, Caleb, what’s the Bible say about suffering?” they’ll ask. Caleb and Carina then have the opportunity to share the Christian perspective. IMB missionaries Caleb and Carina Beaty and their children pose for a photo in a park in Madrid, Spain.  IMB Photo Spain has secularized rapidly since the 1990s, Caleb said. While many may think of it as a Catholic nation, many people do not know the basic tenets of Christianity. “We’ve got all the churches, we’ve got the cathedrals, and they do processions, but the average person on the street does not know anything about the gospel and does not know anything about Jesus,” Caleb said. Younger Spaniards are drawn to their group and are receptive to the gospel because they don’t have a spiritual foundation or know anyone who does. “There’s just this curiosity because, for a lot of them, they’ve never met someone who actually believes that God exists, and that changes your life,” Carina said. “I’ve had people completely shocked that we believe in God. ‘You really believe that God exists?’ They can’t wrap their mind around that.” During one Meetup, a man contrasted Protestant and Catholic beliefs by saying Protestants focus on Jesus’ suffering and Catholics on Mary’s grief. Caleb responded that evangelicals focus on the resurrection. When Caleb said Jesus rose from the dead, the man replied that he needed to look into that. Caleb said encounters like that reveal how little many Spaniards know about the gospel. Caleb noted the irony of the man’s sharing the Catholic perspective without truly understanding it. He is not the only person the Beatys have met who has missed the heart of the gospel. A friend of the Beatys told them she’d heard Jesus died, but she hadn’t heard he rose from the dead. A man reads a passage of Scripture during a Bible study hosted by IMB missionaries Caleb and Carina Beaty at their family’s apartment in Madrid, Spain. Five atheists began attending their Bible study after attending the couple’s Meetup group. IMB Photo The Beatys also host seasonal outreach events through the Meetup. Members from their church in Madrid have started attending the Meetup to learn how the Beatys lead discussions. Their group has become so popular, a waitlist has formed. Caleb and Carina host a small-group Bible study in their home. Five atheists who joined their Meetup now attend the Bible study.

articles.content: IMB Graphic NASHVILLE – As the books closed on the latest fiscal year, receipts for the two Southern Baptist national annual missions offerings underscored the value Southern Baptist churches place on reaching the world with the gospel. The Lottie Moon Christmas Offering® (LMCO) totaled $212.5 million to support International Mission Board (IMB) missionaries, and the Annie Armstrong Easter Offering® (AAEO) reached $73.6 million to support the North American Mission Board’s (NAMB) church planting, compassion ministry and other evangelistic efforts to reach North America. IMB President Paul Chitwood said he celebrates what God did in the 2025-26 season and what He is doing now to lead Southern Baptists toward historic generosity. “I thank God for Southern Baptists! With giving through the Lottie Moon offering at an all-time high, churches and individual givers continue to display a heart for the gospel to be proclaimed to every nation, all tribes, peoples and languages,” Chitwood said. The Annie total marked the second highest in NAMB’s history. The record Lottie Moon offering total surpassed last year’s total by more than $5 million and is the best offering in IMB history. “God is giving our generation unprecedented opportunity to send missionaries to the most unreached peoples and places,” Chitwood continued. “Though the challenges faced by our missionaries are enormous, the generosity of Southern Baptists ensures they have what they need to face those challenges and continue in the work while we hold the ropes with our support.” IMB missionary Landon Williams (center) walks with a Chilean pastor and a U.S. pastor on a remote island in Chile. Cooperation and generosity among Southern Baptists fuels the work to reach the uttermost parts of the world with the gospel. IMB Photo National goals for both offerings are set in partnership with Woman’s Missionary Union (WMU) each year. In response to the offering totals, Sandy Wisdom-Martin, executive director-treasurer of WMU, said: “As Southern Baptists, we are all in for His mission. When we give sacrificially, we prioritize the mission of God. Together our fervent prayers, our faithful generosity and our wholehearted obedience become channels for the gospel to reach our neighbors as well as the nations.” For the last 10 years, Southern Baptists have increasingly supported the Annie offering, setting records in seven of the last 10 years. Totals in each of the last four years have surpassed $70 million. “I am so grateful to the pastors and churches for the faithfulness and generosity they have demonstrated through this offering,” said NAMB president Kevin Ezell. “As I travel and speak in churches of all sizes, I love seeing the posters in the hallways showing their offering goals. For some it is a few hundred dollars, for others several thousand.” The Annie Armstrong offering supports more than 3,000 missionaries in North America, including the ongoing work of church planting in the U.S. and Canada. In 2025, Southern Baptists planted the largest number of churches, 699, since 2016. Including church plants and replants, Southern Baptists have surpassed 700 new churches in four of the last five years. More than 12,000 churches have been planted since 2010. To go along with the increased giving totals to the SBC’s missions offerings, Southern Baptists have also increased their local outreach efforts, indicating that the focus is not just on giving but on sending. Baptism totals have increased in each of the last five years, recovering from the pandemic-year low in 2020 to surpass the 2017 total. The five consecutive years of increase marked the first such streak in approximately 75 years. IMB Photo The chapel at Council Road Baptist Church in Oklahoma City turned into a science lab on Oct. 5-6. Microscopes, beakers and test tubes weren’t in the room, but this Sending Church Lab drew nearly 40 people representing 12 Oklahoma Baptist churches committed to send and care for international missionaries well. The Sending Church Lab, facilitated by the International Mission Board, brought pastors, church leaders and missionaries together for two days of discussion, self-assessment and planning centered on one question: What does it mean for a church to truly be a sending church? For Mike Wall, a global missions ministry partner of Oklahoma Baptists, the answer begins with churches reclaiming responsibility for the Great Commission. Wall first attended a Sending Church Lab last year in Tulsa with few expectations. He left convinced more churches needed the training. “When I went there, I thought, ‘You’ve got to do this in Oklahoma City,’” Wall said, “because of the content and how much our churches need something just like this.” After observing churches work through the exercises in the lab, Wall said he was encouraged by an emphasis on local church ownership in missions. “We can’t just send our people and say, ‘OK, now this is your job, IMB,’” he said. “We have to do our job in sending, preparing and training the best ‘sent ones’ so that when they get to the field, they can already hit the ground running.” Bryan Wooten, IMB senior church engagement specialist, leads a Sending Church Lab at Council Road Baptist Church in Oklahoma City. He is emphasizing the importance of sending churches assessing and equipping future IMB missionaries. IMB Photo Leading the lab was Bryan Wooten, IMB senior church engagement strategist, who developed the concept after seeing the need for stronger relationships between missionaries and local churches. “A Sending Church Lab is our attempt to raise up a host of IMB sending churches,” Wooten said, crediting the North American Mission Board for doing similar events and having successful results. The lab helps churches understand what Wooten calls the church engagement pathway: praying, cooperating, partnering and sending. While many churches faithfully pray, give and go, he said sending requires something more intentional. “Sending includes taking responsibility for an IMB missionary by providing ongoing encouragement, accountability and soul care throughout their term of service,” he explained. During the two-day event, participants gathered around whiteboards to evaluate their church’s missions practices, identify strengths and weaknesses and develop plans for improvement. “We don’t just need to deliver content,” Wooten said. “We need to invite churches to do some work on their own.” Rather than simply listening to presentations, attendees worked through practical questions about prayer, giving, short-term missions, missionary assessment and long-term care. Wooten said churches consistently tell him the greatest benefit is clarity. “They are thankful for clarity on what an IMB sending church is and what our roles and responsibilities are,” he said. Katie appreciated the interactive nature of the training. “I really appreciate the way they’re actually requiring information from the different churches and encouraging dialogue about how they can go through the steps,” she said. articles.title_zh: 数字化之门为东南亚岛民打开福音之门
articles.content: Just as young people today have become more comfortable with talking online than in person, the same is true for people in Southeast Asia. IMB missionaries are creating and publishing Jesus-focused ads, videos and other digital content to connect with the lost through the internet. IMB Photo Recently, an International Mission Board team in Southeast Asia asked a young woman if she had heard the story of Jesus. She replied that, yes, she had heard about Him through a video online! “Back in the day,” shared Amanda Clarkston, an IMB missionary who has served in Southeast Asia for 33 years, “when I first came on the field, you’d go somewhere and gather all the people together in the village to watch the JESUS film.” Now, face-to-face conversations about Christ on the Southeast Asian islands are harder to accomplish. While teams travel to these remote islands often, living in a sparsely populated, animistic background culture as a foreigner creates suspicion and make long-term ministry difficult. Furthermore, young people today have become more comfortable with talking online than they are in person, Clarkston said, which is true of the islanders as well. Attempting to have a spiritual conversation face-to-face has become “too much” for locals, Clarkston shared. So, how do you share the gospel with multiple people groups who are constantly online and less comfortable with in-person interactions? For these Southeast Asia teams, digital engagement — the use of social media platforms to share a message — has become a plausible and effective entry point. The social media agency We Are Social confirmed this, revealing that 82.4% of Southeast Asia’s population uses the internet. “No matter where they go, how far they go, how remote it is, people have phones,” Clarkston and her team realized, “And though sometimes they do have to climb up the highest peak to get reception, people do it.” Clarkston’s team has begun creating and publishing Jesus-focused ads, videos and other digital content in hopes of building bridges to the islanders through the internet. Viewers can click on the ad to message back and forth with a responder, a local believer or missionary who is available to pray, build relationships and answer spiritual questions. “It seems like locals are more open to watching those things in the privacy of their own cell phones,” Clarkston said. Clarkston intends to use digital engagement as a means for initial contact with people with animistic backgrounds, evangelism and, eventually, discipleship. She said that this new ministry has the potential to open doors with individuals across these islands who would normally never reach out on their own or respond to the gospel in person. “Maybe they’ll respond this way,” Clarkston said, “I know without a shadow of a doubt that God is calling people to Himself.” Now, more than ever, technology has a grip on society. Many spend hours each day mindlessly scrolling, searching for meaning, for happiness. And now, more than ever, there is an incredible opportunity to plant seeds across Southeast Asian islands through digital engagement. The IMB Southeast Asia team gives praise to the Lord that He has provided a creative way to reach the lost and plant seeds. Pray the people among the Southeast Asian islands would see these ads and engage with responders boldly, even though they may face persecution or harm because of it. Names were changed for security. articles.content: Ask most people what comes to mind when they think of South Korea, and they’ll likely mention K-pop, skincare, cutting-edge technology, or bustling city streets filled with young professionals. Hun and Eunjoo Sol see those things too. But after more than a decade serving as International Mission Board missionaries in Seoul, they also see something many visitors never notice. “Many people think that Korea is exciting and successful,” Hun said. “They think about the K-pop, the K-culture, K-technology, K-cosmetics. Yes, good things… But many Korean people are struggling right now.” The Sols, who were featured in the 2025 Week of Prayer for International Missions , continue to rely on the prayers of faithful Southern Baptists. Prayers sustain them and help to push back the darkness they confront in their home culture. Hun often describes that hidden struggle with a Korean word: han. There is no simple English translation. It speaks to a deep sorrow shaped by generations of war, division, loss, and the quiet resolve to endure. Hun sees it in the young adults he meets every week—people navigating loneliness and relentless expectations, quietly asking what their lives are for beneath a veneer of success. Han is heavy. For many young adults, that weight can feel unbearable. Suicide is one of the leading causes of death among teenagers and young adults in South Korean. Hun and Eunjoo see the effects of that reality every day, and it’s one reason they believe they have no time to waste. That understanding shaped the week of Serve Tour Seoul this summer. There were no construction sites, no paintbrushes, no tools or work gloves. Instead, the team stepped into ministries local churches had been faithfully building long before the volunteers arrived. In May, 27 volunteers from seven churches across the United States came alongside local churches already serving their communities in Seoul, Paju, and Gwangju. They taught English classes, ran children’s camps, walked neighborhoods in prayer, distributed food, and sat down with college students, one conversation at a time. For Nick Holst of Sandals Church in Riverside, California, the goal was simple enough to say in a sentence: “We came to meet people,” Holst said. “We want to hear their stories, and that leads to some very meaningful connections as you get past the surface into something deeper.” That’s where the week actually lived: past the surface and past the small talk, where the quiet weight of han is often carried without words. On college campuses, volunteers played games, asked questions and mostly just listened. Some conversations lasted a few minutes and ended there. Others kept going long past the point where either person expected them to. One morning, after asking his church back home to pray, Holst sat down with a university student named Intec. They talked about culture first, the way strangers do, and then the conversation turned somewhere neither of them planned. “I got to ask him, ‘What do Koreans believe?’” Holst recalled. Intec said he didn’t believe in God. Then he recited John 3:16 from memory, word for word, a verse he’d heard somewhere along the way and never forgotten. Before they parted, Holst asked if he could pray that God would keep drawing Intec toward Himself. “He said yes.” In a city where many conversations never move beyond the surface, the exchange was a reminder of why the team had come. Not to win an argument, but to listen, to ask questions, and to trust God with what happens next. The same pattern unfolded elsewhere, beginning in classrooms and ending on city streets. Jeremy Doyle, missions pastor at Valley Baptist Church in Bakersfield, California, watched an English conversation club grow from two students on its first night to eight by the second. articles.title: A construction engineer in Madagascar became convinced the Bible was true
articles.summary: 🇲🇬Madagascar· 2013

articles.title_zh: 一位在马达加斯加的建筑工程师确信圣经是真的
articles.content: Melias was building things for a living in Madagascar, a construction engineer with a steady trade and, by his own account, no particular expectation that God would interrupt him. In 2013, at twenty-one, God did. It was not dramatic thunder. It was quieter and harder to argue with. "The Holy Spirit convinced my heart that the Bible is true," Melias said. "I found new joy and excitement learning about Jesus through the Scriptures." The book he might have dismissed became the most alive thing in his life. From building houses to building the church He could have kept his new faith as a private comfort and gone on with engineering. Instead he gave it everything. In 2015 he trained for six months as a missionary, and since then he has planted churches and discipled new believers among the Tanala people in Ikongo and the Sakalava in Nosy Be, some of the least reached corners of the island. Now he is training three more Malagasy missionaries to do the same. Madagascar is not a footnote in what God is doing. He is raising up local people like Melias, engineers and tradesmen and ordinary workers, and sending them to their own unreached neighbours. When the Holy Spirit convinces your heart that this is all true, it does not stay a hobby. It becomes the thing you build your life around. He is ready to convince yours.
articles.content_zh:
梅利亚斯在马达加斯加为生计而建东西,他是一位稳定的建筑工程师,据他自己说,他并不特别期望上帝会打断他。 2013年,21时,上帝做到了. 这不是戏剧性的雷声。 更安静,更难争论 "圣灵使我的心相信圣经是真的,"梅利亚斯说.

"我发现新的快乐和兴奋 通过圣经学习耶稣。" 他可能放弃的书 成为他一生中最活的 从建房到建教堂 他本可以保持他作为私人慰藉的新信仰,继续从事工程工作. 相反,他给了它一切。

2015年,他作为传教士接受了半年的训练,此后他在伊孔戈的塔纳拉人和诺西贝的萨卡拉瓦人中种植了教堂和门徒新信徒,其中部分到达的岛角最少. 现在他正在训练另外三名马达加斯加传教士, 马达加斯加不是上帝所作所为的一个脚注。

他正在培养梅利亚斯,工程师和商人以及普通工人等当地人,并将他们送到他们自己无法接触到的邻居那里. 当圣灵说服你的心脏 这一切都是真的, 它不仍然是爱好。 它成为你围绕你生活的东西。 他准备说服你

articles.title: A New Testament sat in his welding workshop until a teenager finally read it
articles.summary: 🇳🇪Agadez· 2000s
articles.summary_zh: 🇳🇪阿加德兹·21世纪初
articles.title_zh: 一本新约圣经一直放在他的焊接车间里，直到一位少年终于读了它。
articles.content: Someone left a New Testament in Pierre's welding workshop in Niger, and for a while it just sat there. He was a teenager, and eventually he picked it up. What he read did not match what he had been told about Christians. It was full of tenderness, of nearness to the poorest, exactly the kind of world his young heart had been quietly hoping was real. Years later he moved to Agadez, out toward the desert, and there he found the thing the book had described. A church family drawn from Benin, Togo, Burkina Faso, France, and Niger, living out what he had only read about. No regret, not for a single day Pierre became a lay missionary, and he does not hedge when he talks about it. "I have never regretted converting to the Christian faith," he says, "not even for a single day." That is a bold thing to say in Niger, where jihadist groups make following Jesus dangerous and his own children have stayed Muslim, something he carries with love and without pressure. Still, no regret. Not one day. He read about a God who is tender toward the poor, and he found that God to be exactly as advertised. Whatever you have heard about Jesus secondhand, He holds up when you finally meet Him yourself. Pierre would tell you to open the book and see.
articles.content_zh:
有人在尼日尔的皮埃尔焊接车间留下了一份新约, 他少年时期,最终他捡到了. 他所读的内容与他被告知的基督徒的情况不符。 它充满了温柔,与最贫穷的人的亲近, 正是他年轻时所希望的世界是真实的。

多年后,他搬到阿加德兹, 向着沙漠, 在那里他发现了书上描述的东西。 一个来自贝宁、多哥、布基纳法索、法国和尼日尔的教会家庭,靠他只读过的东西生活。 没有遗憾,没有一天,皮埃尔成为了一名非专业的传教士,他谈论这件事时不设套.

"我从未后悔过皈依基督教信仰",他说:"即使是一天也没有". 在尼日尔,这是一件大胆的事,在那里,圣战团体追随耶稣,而他自己的孩子则留在穆斯林手中,他带着爱,没有压力。 不过,没有遗憾。 一日不见.

他曾诵读了真主--对于贫民是温和的--他发现真主确是彻知的。 无论你听到什么关于耶稣的二手消息 当你们终于亲眼见到他时 他都挺过来了 Pierre会告诉你打开书看看

articles.content: Pastor Peter Colon portraying Major Rossvally in the movie of his story By Charles Gardner — A Jewish army surgeon was amazed by the courage of a young soldier badly wounded in the Battle of Gettysburg during the American Civil War (1861-65). Dr Max Rossvally was forced to amputate both a leg and arm in a bid to save the boy’s life. But it changed his own life. For the 17-year-old Drummer Boy – too young for frontline duty – refused chloroform or brandy to dull the pain. Charlie Coulson chose instead to trust in Jesus, his Lord and Saviour. The doctor – an army major and Orthodox Jew – was understandably stunned by the boy’s bravery, as well as his boldness in declaring his faith in Christ and imploring the officer (whom he knew to be Jewish) to put his own trust in Jesus, since he was also the Jewish Messiah. Max, however, was shaken rigid, and in a great dilemma, as he had always been taught to hate Jesus. For his people had largely rejected him as an ‘impostor’ and false Messiah. Charlie died just days later, apparently more concerned for the doctor’s eternal destiny than for his own painful exit from this life. Ten years later, Max found himself in a barber’s chair in New York once more being urged to trust in Jesus. Having explained the gospel, the barber promised to pray for him and said that, whenever he came in contact with a Jew, he felt it his duty to introduce him to the one who came for “the lost sheep of Israel” (Matthew 10:6). The surgeon subsequently boarded a train for a business meeting in Washington, where a newspaper advertisement drew him to a ‘revival’ service where the preacher echoed the messages he had heard from the barber and the boy soldier, leaving him in tears. He agonised at home in prayer for some time afterwards, struggling most of all with the thought that, if he accepted Christ, he would be going against all the advice and teaching he had known, not to mention the Jewish community as a whole. But he finally became convinced that Jesus was indeed the fulfilment of Old Testament prophecies (in particular, Genesis 49:10, Micah 5:2 and Isaiah 7:14). So he prayed: “O Lord God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. You know I am sincere in this thing. If Jesus Christ is the Son of God, reveal him to me this night, and I will accept him as my Messiah.” A long battle ensued, but his doubts were eventually replaced by joy and happiness as he praised God that he had found the true Shiloh, Ruler of Israel and Emmanuel. He was to pay a high price, however, as do all who follow Christ. His wife walked out on him; his parents disowned him. But he never gave up hope as he constantly prayed and reached out to his family. After 54 days, his wife joined him as a disciple of Jesus and, in time, his daughter also became a believer. But his son disowned him for many years until he was eventually reconciled both with his earthly and heavenly Father. In an extraordinary sequel some 18 months after he came to Christ, Max met up with Mrs Coulson, the mother of his dying young patient all those years earlier on the battlefield. With great joy, he was able to share how her son had set him on the path to a glorious future in Christ, which was to touch lives across the world, including my home county of Yorkshire in England. In fact, he came to live in Leeds to reach out to the Jewish community there and is buried at Lawnswood Cemetery in the city. An Irish friend of mine, Colin Nevin, has visited the grave, which includes an excerpt from one of the doctor’s hymns, I am Coming Soon, and was able to give a copy of Max’s story to a caretaker, so continuing the evangelist’s legacy more than a century after his death in 1892, aged 64. A 54-minute movie – Rossvally: From the Synagogue to the Saviour – has been produced on DVD and can apparently be ordered online. 牧师彼得·科隆在他的故事电影"查尔斯·加德纳"(By Charles Gardner)中描绘了罗斯瓦利少校——一位犹太军队外科医生对美国内战期间格底斯堡战役(1861-65)中一名年轻士兵严重受伤的勇气感到惊讶. Max Rossvally医生被迫截肢, 但这改变了他自己的生活。

对于17岁的Drummer Boy — — 年龄太小,无法承担前线任务 — — 拒绝氯仿或白兰地来消磨疼痛。 查理·科尔森选择了信任耶稣,他的主和救世主.

这位医生是一名陆军少校和正统犹太人,对男孩的勇敢以及他大胆地宣布对基督的信仰,恳求军官(他知道是犹太人)相信耶稣是可以理解的,因为他也是犹太弥赛亚。 然而,马克思被动摇僵硬,陷入了巨大的困境,因为他一直被教导要憎恨耶稣.

他的宗族曾否认他是一个 " 骗子 " 和假的弥赛亚。 Charlie在几天后就去世了,显然更关心医生的永恒命运,而不是他自己痛苦地离开这一生。 10年后,马克思发现自己在纽约的理发师座椅上再次被敦促信任耶稣.

在解释了福音之后,理发师答应为他祈祷,并说每当他与一个犹太人接触时,他觉得有义务将他介绍给前来寻找“迷失的以色列羊”的人(Matthew 10:6)。

外科医生随后登上火车在华盛顿举行商务会议,报纸的广告将他引向 " 复活 " 服务,传教士重复了他从理发师和男孩士兵那里听到的信息,使他流泪。

他在家里苦苦地祈祷了一段时间,他首先想到,如果他接受基督,他将反对他所知道的所有建议和教导,更不用说整个犹太社区了。 但他最终确信耶稣确实是"旧约预言"的实现(特别是创世纪49:10,米迦5:2和以赛亚7:14).

他就祈祷说:易卜拉欣、易司哈格、叶尔孤白的主啊! 你知道我对这件事很真诚 如果耶稣基督是上帝之子,那么今晚把他告诉我,我将接受他为我的弥赛亚。” 一场漫长的战斗随之而来,但他的疑虑最终被欢乐和幸福所取代,因为他称赞上帝找到了真正的希洛,以色列统治者和埃马纽埃尔.

但他要付出高昂的代价,跟随基督的所有人一样。 他的妻子抛弃了他;他的父母抛弃了他。 但是,他从未放弃过希望,因为他不断祈祷和联系家人。 在54天后,他的妻子作为耶稣的门徒加入了他,在时间上,他的女儿也成为了信徒.

但他的儿子与他断绝关系多年,直到他最终与他的大地父和天父都和解. 在他来到基督的大约18个月之后的一段非凡续集中,马克思在战场上遇见了那些年前他死去的年轻病人的母亲科尔森夫人.

他怀着极大的喜悦,得以分享她儿子如何使他踏上基督辉煌未来的道路,这就是触摸世界各地的生活,包括我的家乡英格兰约克郡. 事实上,他来到利兹居住,向那里的犹太社区伸出援手,并被埋在城内的草坪林墓地.

我的一个爱尔兰朋友科林·内文参观了这个坟墓,其中包括医生颂歌"I am Coming Soon"的节录,并且能够把马克思的故事复制给看守人,因此在1892年去世后一个多世纪的福音派传承下来,享年64岁.

一部54分钟的电影 — — Rossvally: 从Synagogue到救世主 — 已经在DVD上制作,显然可以在网上订购. 在目睹病人的勇气首次出现在上帝的报告之后,

上次我听到布鲁斯·雷德福德教授 谈到古怪的英国神职人员和诗人克里斯托弗·斯马特(1722–1771)时,我受到很大启发,在[.]中包含了一大部分斯马特非凡的诗歌,大庆阿格诺. 以及《信仰之诗》,
articles.title_zh: 喜悦羔羊：本杰明·布里顿、克里斯托弗·斯马特和信仰的诗歌
articles.content: When music meets poetry, the result can be more than art, it can become an expression of spiritual wonder. Christopher Smart The last time I heard Professor Bruce Redford speak about the eccentric British clergyman and poet Christopher Smart (1722–1771), I was so inspired that I included a substantial portion of Smart’s extraordinary poem, Jubilate Agno , in my book Beauty (And the Banana) . I described Smart as a theopoet , someone whose deep religious convictions found expression through a distinctive and imaginative poetic vision. Smart was no ordinary poet. His writings moved freely between the sacred and the seemingly mundane, finding divine significance in everything from biblical figures to animals and the natural world. His poetry was exuberant, unconventional, and, at times, wonderfully strange. For Smart, creation itself was a chorus of praise, and every living thing had a part to play. Recently, I had another opportunity to hear Redford explore Smart’s remarkable literary legacy, this time through the music of British composer Benjamin Britten (1913–1976). As part of an All Saints’ Day concert at the Cathedral of St. John in Albuquerque, New Mexico, celebrating Britten’s music, Redford delivered a pre-concert lecture focusing on the composer’s Rejoice in the Lamb , a choral masterpiece that brings Smart’s unusual poetry to life. The evening offered a fascinating intersection of literature, music, theology, and history, demonstrating how two artists separated by nearly two centuries could share a common vision of wonder. The Musical Imagination of Benjamin Britten Benjamin Britten. Photo: Public Domain. Redford, a former professor at Boston University who was living in England when Britten died in 1976, identified three defining characteristics of the composer’s work. First, Britten’s music is distinguished by “passion and variety.” His compositions resist easy categorization, moving between emotional intensity, dramatic storytelling, and moments of remarkable spiritual intimacy. Redford described Britten’s approach as creating a kind of musical parable, pointing to Curlew River , one of Britten’s church parables, as a particularly compelling example. Second, Britten demonstrated an extraordinary ability to balance “economy and scope.” Redford compared this quality to the novels of Jane Austen, whose carefully constructed narratives reveal entire worlds through seemingly modest details. Similarly, Britten could communicate profound emotional and spiritual truths through restrained musical means. Nothing was wasted; every note served a purpose. Third, and perhaps most important for the evening’s performance, Britten possessed an exceptional “sensitivity to words.” Redford described him as an “inspired” interpreter of literary texts, a composer who understood that music should not merely accompany poetry but illuminate its deeper meaning. It was this third characteristic that led Redford to Christopher Smart. When an Eccentric Poet Meets a Brilliant Composer In 1943, Britten composed Rejoice in the Lamb (Op. 30), a festival cantata scored for four soloists, SATB choir, and organ. The composition draws its text from Smart’s Jubilate Agno , a work of religious poetry that remained largely unknown for nearly two centuries. Christopher Smart Smart wrote much of the poem during his confinement in a private madhouse in eighteenth-century London. Its unconventional structure, biblical references, exuberant language, and seemingly spontaneous declarations of praise made it unlike almost anything else in English religious literature. The manuscript remained unpublished until W. F. Stead brought it to public attention in 1939. Soon afterward, the poet W. H. Auden introduced Britten to Smart’s newly published work while the composer was living in the United States. The connection proved fruitful. Britten recognized something remarkable in Smart’s poetry: an unrestrained celebration of creation that could be translated into music.
articles.content_zh:
当音乐与诗歌相遇时,结果可以超越艺术,成为精神奇迹的体现. 克里斯托弗·聪明 上次我听到布鲁斯·雷德福德教授谈到古怪的英国神职人员和诗人克里斯托弗·斯马特(1722–1771)时,我深受启发,在我的书《美人(和香蕉)》中包含了一大部分斯马特非凡的诗集《阿格诺大庆》。

我形容Smart是一位戏剧家, 聪明不是普通诗人 他的著作在圣人和看似庸俗的人之间自由移动,在从圣经人物到动物和自然世界的一切事物中都发现了神圣的意义.

他的诗歌充满了活力,与众不同,有时也非常奇怪. 对于Smart来说,创作本身是赞美的合唱,每一个活物都有角色可以扮演. 最近,我又有机会听到雷德福德探索Smart杰出的文学遗产,这次是通过英国作曲家本杰明·布里顿的音乐(1913–1976).

作为新墨西哥州阿尔布开克圣约翰大教堂庆祝布列顿音乐的全圣人节音乐会的一部分,雷德福德发表了一场音乐会前演讲,重点讲述了作曲家在羊羔中的欢乐,这是一部将斯马特不寻常的诗歌带给人生的奇特杰作.

晚上提供了文学、音乐、神学和历史的奇妙交汇点,展示了两个艺术家如何在将近两个世纪的时间里分开,可以分享一个共同的奇观。 本杰明·布林顿·本杰明·布林顿的音乐想象. 图片:公共域名.

雷德福德(Redford)是波士顿大学前教授,1976年布里顿逝世时居住在英国,他确定了作曲家作品的三个决定性特征. 首先,布列顿的音乐以“热情和多样性”来区分。 他的构思抵制轻松的分类,在情感的强度,戏剧性的故事性,以及非凡的精神亲密的时刻之间移动.

Redford将布列顿的做法描述为创造了一种音乐比喻,指向了布列顿教堂比喻之一的Curlew River,作为特别有说服力的例子.

第二,Britten表现出了平衡“经济和范围”的非凡能力。 雷德福德将这种品质与简·奥斯汀的小说相比较,他精心构建的叙事通过看似微小的细节揭示了整个世界. 同样,布列顿可以通过受约束的音乐手段传达深刻的情感和精神真理. 没有浪费任何东西;每张纸条都有作用。

第三,或许对晚间演出来说最重要的,布列顿拥有一种非凡的“言语敏感性 ” 。 Redford将他描述为文学文本的“受启发的”解释者,他是一个作曲家,他明白音乐不应仅仅伴随着诗歌,而应阐明其更深层次的意义。 正是这第三个特征导致雷德福找到克里斯托弗·斯马特.

1943年,当一位爱心诗人遇到一位杰出的作曲家时,布列顿在"羔羊"(Op. 30)中编曲了"欢乐"(Rejoice in the Lamb (Op. 30)),一个节日的Cantata为四位独奏家,SATB合唱团和管风琴打分. 内容来自Smart's Jubilate Agno, 一部宗教诗歌作品,

克里斯托弗·斯马特(Christopher Smart Smart)在18世纪伦敦一个私人疯人院禁闭期间写下了这首诗的大部分内容. 它的非常规结构,圣经的参考文献,兴旺的语言,以及看似自发的赞美宣言,使得它几乎不同于英国宗教文献中的其他任何内容. 手稿直到W. F.

施泰德在1939年引起了公众的注意. 不久之后,诗人W·H·奥登(W. H. Auden)在作曲家在美国居住期间,向布里顿介绍了斯马特新出版的作品. 这种联系证明是富有成果的。 Britten在Smart的诗歌中承认了一些令人瞩目的事物:一种可以被翻译成音乐的无限制的创作庆典.

The most relevant of his teaching to current events is his view of Iran. Based on his study of Daniel 7, Daniel 8 and Revelation 6, Davidson identified four major events, which he calls “signposts,” that he believes will unfold in the Middle East before the Tribulation. 马克·埃利斯 作为10岁的男孩,马克·戴维森的母亲给了他Hal Lindsey的书"晚大星球地球"(The Late Great Planet Earth),这本书最终售出约3500万份,被纽约时报宣布为1970年代最畅销的非小说书籍. 该书对戴维森影响很大,塑造了他对"圣经预言"末期最早的看法.

“他们都在谈论相同的四个事件, 他表示,第一个路标在伊拉克政府在2003年到2005年间更换时就已经实现,他现在认为,涉及霍尔木兹海峡的伊朗冲突与破坏可能表明第二个路标正在开始展开。 第二个路标是伊朗(Shia)攻击逊尼派邻国。

他偏离了传统教义,认为即将到来的反基督者将是阿拉伯叙利亚穆斯林。 他认为,“这十个王国不是罗马王国;它们是穆斯林王国,从摩洛哥延伸到巴基斯坦。” 有些人在Davidson的网站上发表评论,

articles.title_zh: Patrick Nagatani：通过色彩、摄影和艺术进行的精神探索
articles.content: Arriving in Albuquerque, New Mexico, in 2009, I was fortunate to catch the final chapter of artist and photographer Patrick Nagatani’ s remarkable career before his death from cancer in 2017. As one of my favorite modern photographers, Nagatani fascinated me with his unique artistic vision, his imaginative compositions, and his ability to transform his photography into extraordinary works of art. Watching him at gallery openings was a pleasure. He was cordial, kind, and genuinely responsive to those who engaged him. There was something refreshing about an artist of his stature who remained approachable, thoughtful, and seemingly delighted to discuss his work. An Artist Shaped by History Photo credit: Grahm Howe, 1979. Patrick Ryoichi Nagatani was born on August 19, 1945, in Chicago, Illinois, only days after the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki. His Japanese American parents had experienced incarceration during World War II, and the legacy of displacement, cultural identity, and nuclear destruction would profoundly influence his artistic imagination. Raised Catholic, Nagatani eventually moved with his family to Los Angeles. He studied at UCLA, earning his Master of Fine Arts in 1980. His early professional experience included model-making for Hollywood productions, helping establish the theatrical techniques that later distinguished his photography. In 1987, he moved to Albuquerque to teach at the University of New Mexico , where he became an influential professor and internationally recognized artist. His celebrated Nuclear Enchantment series examined the disturbing relationship between New Mexico’s landscapes and the nuclear industry. articles.content: An IMB missionary among the Deaf records a Bible story in sign language. IMB Photo Every dollar you give to the Lottie Moon offering goes to support missionaries like Noah Lewis who live and serve among the lost. Will you consider giving today? Noah Lewis couldn’t help signing along with a worship song playing in the background as Deaf friends gathered in his home for dinner. The International Mission Board appoints missionaries who are both Deaf and hearing to serve among the global Deaf. Many missionaries learn sign language for the first time, while others use their American Sign Language to more quickly learn global sign languages. IMB Photo The International Mission Board missionary was sitting in the living room with his roommate and two friends while others prepared food nearby. As a young, single adult, simply opening the doors to his home in the Middle East has created some of his most fruitful opportunities for gospel conversations. That evening, Lewis was stirred to worship the Lord. “I just love worshiping in sign language because it’s a full-body experience,” Lewis said. Lewis, who is hearing, began signing the song in American Sign Language. Across the room, one of his Muslim friends watched intently. When the song ended, his friend told him it was beautiful and asked to see another. Lewis explained that Christians use songs to worship God. His friend compared what he had seen to hearing the Islamic call to prayer. The exchange opened an opportunity for Lewis to explain Christian worship and why Christians worship Jesus. When his friend asked to see more, Lewis continued signing songs from the playlist. “He was just really captivated by it,” Lewis said. “It really felt like in that moment the Spirit was working in his heart.” The conversation did not end with a profession of faith. Instead, it became another step in a friendship where Lewis has watched spiritual curiosity grow over time. During Ramadan, the same friend asked about fasting. On another night, he asked how Christians pray. Each question has allowed Lewis to explain what Christians believe and why he follows Jesus. Those conversations reflect much of Lewis’ ministry. He has served in the Middle East for nearly a year and a half, spending much of his time learning sign language and building relationships in the local Deaf community. Learning sign language, like learning any language, requires time, practice and immersion in the community that uses it. For Lewis, that process has looked different from the experience of missionaries who can spend several hours each day in a formal language school. There are no comparable sign language centers where he serves, so much of his language learning happens through relationships with Deaf friends. Although Lewis has not had a dedicated language tutor since arriving on the field, personal relationships help him develop a strong conversational understanding of the sign language used where he serves. The process has also drawn him more deeply into the Deaf community he came to reach. “I want to genuinely learn about their language,” he said. “I want to be friends with them. I want to know who they are.” As Lewis’ ability to communicate grows, relationships deepen and opportunities to share the gospel follow. Even when he doesn’t know the exact sign he needs, friends help him find ways to communicate biblical truths. Lewis has learned to faithfully use the language he has while continuing to grow in his ability to communicate the gospel clearly. An IMB worker among the Deaf records a Bible story. 国际代表团委员会任命聋人和听力传教士在全球聋人中任职。 许多传教士首次学习手语,而其他传教士则使用他们的美国手语更快地学习全球手语.

IMB照片 国际传教委员会传教士与他的室友和两个朋友坐在客厅里,而其他人则在附近准备食物. 作为一个年轻、单身的成年人,只要打开通往他在中东的家的大门,就为他的福音对话创造了一些最富有成果的机会。 当晚,刘易斯被激起崇拜主.

「我只是喜欢手语崇拜, 正在听话的刘易斯开始用美国手语签署歌曲. 在房间里,他的一个穆斯林朋友故意观看。 歌曲结束的时候,他的朋友告诉他这很美丽,并请求见另一首. 刘易斯解释说,基督徒使用歌曲来崇拜上帝.

他的朋友比较了他所看到的听到的伊斯兰祈祷的呼声. 这次交流为刘易斯解释基督教崇拜和基督徒为何崇拜耶稣提供了机会. 当他的朋友要求看到更多时,刘易斯继续从播放列表上签名歌曲. 刘易斯说:“他只是被它迷住了。”

“在那个时刻,精神确实在他心中发挥作用。” 对话没有以信仰职业结束。 相反,它成为友谊的又一个步骤,刘易斯目睹了精神好奇心随时间推移而增长. 斋月期间,同友问斋事. 在另一个晚上,他问基督徒如何祈祷.

每个问题都让刘易斯解释基督徒相信什么,为什么他跟随耶稣. 这些谈话反映了刘易斯部的许多情况。 他在中东服务了近一年半,花了很多时间学习手语,在当地聋人社区建立关系.

学习手语,就像学习任何语言一样,需要时间,练习和沉浸在使用手语的社区中. 对刘易斯来说,这一进程与传教士的经历不同,传教士可以每天在一所正式语言学校中度过几个小时。

他所服务的手语中心并不存在类似的手语中心,所以他的许多语言学习都是通过与聋人朋友的关系发生的. 虽然刘易斯自到达球场后便没有专门的语言辅导员,但个人关系帮助他发展出对他所服务的手语的强烈的对话理解.
